title: System calls and mmap
summary: How a program enters the Linux kernel on x86-64, what a syscall costs, how calls block and get interrupted, and how mmap maps files lazily, shares pages between processes and can be traced and sandboxed.
outcomes: Explain how the x86-64 syscall instruction passes the number, arguments and errors between user code and the kernel
Estimate syscall overhead from a per-call cost and cut it with buffering, batching and the vDSO
Compute which page a mapped byte lands in and predict zero-fill, SIGBUS and EINVAL cases for a file mapping
Explain MAP_SHARED, MAP_PRIVATE, MAP_ANONYMOUS and copy-on-write, including when writes reach the file
Decide when mmap beats explicit I/O and when a buffer pool is the safer design
Write read and write loops that survive blocking, short counts, EINTR and EAGAIN
Predict how munmap, mprotect and mremap edit the VMA list, and share memory between processes with MAP_SHARED, shm_open or memfd
Count system calls and page faults with strace and getrusage, and restrict system calls with a seccomp filter

lessons.title: What happens when your program calls write

blocks.md:
Your program runs in **user mode**: the CPU refuses privileged instructions, and the kernel's memory is off limits. That is what keeps one buggy program from scribbling on the disk controller or on another process. Recall from the virtual memory course that every load and store goes through page tables the kernel owns.

So how does `printf` ever reach the terminal? It asks the kernel. A **system call** (syscall) is a controlled doorway: user code names an operation by number, passes arguments in registers, and executes one special instruction that switches the CPU to kernel mode at an entry point the kernel chose in advance. User code cannot jump anywhere else inside the kernel.

On x86-64 Linux the doorway is the `syscall` instruction. The rules come from [syscall(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/syscall.2.html) and the comment above the kernel's entry code. A name like syscall(2) points to a page of the Linux manual: section 2 covers system calls, section 3 C library functions, section 7 overviews. Below, `rax`, `rdi` and the rest are names of the processor's sixteen 64-bit general-purpose registers.

- `rax` holds the syscall number. Numbers come from the kernel's table: `read` is 0, `write` is 1, `mmap` is 9, `munmap` is 11, `getpid` is 39, `exit` is 60.
- Up to six arguments go in `rdi`, `rsi`, `rdx`, `r10`, `r8`, `r9`.
- The result comes back in `rax`.

A **file descriptor** (fd) is the small integer the kernel hands a process to name an open file; descriptor 1 is standard output, stdout. Here is the whole thing with no C library at all: write 3 bytes to stdout, then exit.

blocks.title: A raw 3-byte write to stdout in x86-64 assembly
blocks.code:
.section .rodata
msg: .ascii "hi\n"
    .text
    .globl _start
_start:
    mov  $1, %eax          # syscall number 1 = write
    mov  $1, %edi          # arg0: fd 1 (stdout)
    lea  msg(%rip), %rsi   # arg1: buffer address
    mov  $3, %edx          # arg2: count = 3 bytes
    syscall                # enter the kernel
    # back in user mode: rax = 3 or -errno
    mov  $60, %eax         # syscall number 60 = exit
    xor  %edi, %edi        # arg0: status 0
    syscall

scenes.caption: Load the syscall number. To the kernel, 1 means write. Nothing has happened yet: this is an ordinary register move in user mode.

Arguments go where the ABI (application binary interface: the calling rules compiled code agrees on) puts them: fd in rdi, buffer pointer in rsi, length in rdx. The kernel will read them from exactly these places.

syscall saves the user return address into rcx and the flags into r11, then jumps to the kernel entry point stored in a model-specific register (MSR), a CPU control register only the kernel can set. The CPU is now in kernel mode.
The kernel ran its write handler and returned. rax now holds the result: 3 bytes written. rcx and r11 hold whatever the CPU put there, so they are clobbered.
Same pattern for exit: number 60 in rax, status in rdi, syscall. This call never returns.

blocks.md: Two traps in the convention. The 4th argument goes in `r10`, not `rcx` as in a normal C call, because the `syscall` instruction itself overwrites `rcx` with the return address. And after the call, `rcx` and `r11` are garbage from your point of view. Compilers know this; hand-written inline assembly must list them as clobbered.

What does the kernel do between `syscall` and the return? In the current source ([entry_64.S](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/arch/x86/entry/entry_64.S)), `entry_SYSCALL_64` runs `swapgs`, which swaps the user value of the GS base register for the kernel's so that GS points at this CPU's own kernel data (per-CPU data), switches to kernel page tables and a kernel stack, and pushes every user register into a `pt_regs` structure. Then `do_syscall_64` checks the number is in range and dispatches to the handler, such as `sys_write`. On the way out it restores the registers and, when the state allows it, returns with the fast `sysretq` instruction, the mirror of `syscall`: it reloads the user instruction pointer from `rcx` and the flags from `r11`.

blocks.title: The path of one write() call

scenes.caption: Your code calls write like any C function. The libc wrapper (libc is the C standard library) is ordinary user-mode code that puts the number and arguments in registers.
The syscall instruction transfers control to entry_SYSCALL_64, the single entry point for 64-bit system calls. The mode switch happens here.
Registers are saved into pt_regs, then do_syscall_64 checks the number against the table size and calls the matching handler.
The handler's return value goes into rax and the kernel returns to the instruction after syscall. Back in user mode.
If rax holds a value from -4095 to -1, the wrapper treats it as an error: it stores the positive code in errno (the C library's per-thread error-code variable) and returns -1 to your code.

blocks.md: The kernel reports errors as small negative numbers in `rax`. The kernel defines `MAX_ERRNO` as 4095, and glibc (the GNU C Library, the usual libc on Linux) checks whether the raw value, compared as an unsigned number, is above -4096; in C that is literally `(unsigned long) val > -4096UL`. Read as an unsigned 64-bit number, -4096 is 2 to the 64 minus 4096, so only raw values from 2 to the 64 minus 4095 up to 2 to the 64 minus 1 pass, and read as signed numbers those are exactly -4095 to -1. Any raw result in that range is an error. 4095 is one less than the 4096-byte page size, so the error codes all sit in the topmost page of addresses, where no user mapping can ever be. The wrapper negates such a result into `errno` and returns -1. So the familiar "returns -1 and sets errno" contract is a C library convention layered over the raw kernel interface.

blocks.prompt: A program calls `write` on fd 7, which it already closed. The raw `syscall` returns -9 in `rax` (`EBADF`, bad file descriptor, is 9). What does the C caller of `write` see?
blocks.reveal: The return value is **-1** and `errno` is **9** (`EBADF`). The wrapper saw a raw value in the range -4095 to -1, negated it into `errno`, and replaced the return value with -1. If you call `syscall(2)` through `syscall()`, the same translation happens. Only a hand-written `syscall` instruction sees the raw -9.

blocks.question: Why does the x86-64 Linux syscall convention pass the 4th argument in r10 instead of rcx, which the normal C calling convention uses?
options: The syscall instruction overwrites rcx with the user return address
The kernel needs rcx to hold the syscall number
r10 is faster to read from kernel mode
rcx is reserved for the error code
blocks.explain: The `syscall` instruction saves the return address in rcx and rflags in r11, so anything you put in rcx is destroyed by the instruction itself. The kernel's entry comment notes that arg3 arrives in r10 and must be moved to rcx to match the C ABI before calling C handlers.

blocks.question: mmap returns a pointer. The raw syscall can also fail. How does libc tell a valid address from an error in rax?
options: A valid address is never negative, so any value with the top bit set is an error
The kernel sets the carry flag on error
Values from -4095 to -1 (the top 4095 addresses) are reserved for errors; anything else is a result
mmap returns 0 on error
blocks.explain: On x86-64 Linux there is no separate error flag (the syscall(2) table lists none). Those top 4095 values lie in the kernel half of the address space, never a user mapping, so glibc treats raw results in that range as negated error codes. Checking the top bit alone would be wrong in general: glibc uses one rule for every call on every architecture, and on 32-bit x86 a valid mapping above 2 GiB has its top bit set.

lessons.title: What a system call costs, and how to make fewer of them

blocks.md:
A function call costs a few cycles. A system call costs far more, in two ways. The **direct cost** is the mode switch itself: entering the kernel, saving state, returning. The **indirect cost** is what the kernel's code and data do to your caches, TLB and branch predictors while it runs: when you come back, your working set has been partly evicted.

The FlexSC paper ("FlexSC: Flexible System Call Scheduling with Exception-Less System Calls", Soares and Stumm, at OSDI 2010, the USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation) measured both on a 2.3 GHz Intel Core i7. A syscall that does nothing took 79 cycles to enter and 71 to leave: **150 cycles round trip**, about 65 ns (150 cycles divided by 2.3 billion cycles per second). After a single `pwrite` (a `write` to a given file offset), the user program's instructions per cycle stayed depressed for up to **14,000 cycles** (about 6.1 microseconds) while it refilled its caches.

blocks.title: Cache lines evicted per call or call group (FlexSC, Core i7)

scenes.caption: L1 instruction-cache lines replaced by the kernel during each call (64-byte lines). Modest: 2 to 5 KB of code.
L1 data-cache (d-cache) lines replaced. The d-cache on that CPU held 32 KB (512 lines), so each call evicts a large fraction of it. This is the indirect cost your code pays after returning.

blocks.md: Treat 150 cycles as a floor from 2010 hardware, not a current number. Since then kernels added mitigations on every entry and exit for CPU vulnerabilities: you can see `SWITCH_TO_KERNEL_CR3` (separate kernel page tables) and `IBRS_ENTER` (IBRS, Indirect Branch Restricted Speculation, limits branch speculation) in today's `entry_SYSCALL_64`. Measure on your own machine before quoting a number.

The direct cost is paid **per call**, not per byte. So the main lever is to make fewer calls that each do more. Writing 1 MiB one byte at a time takes 1,048,576 `write` calls. With a 4 KiB buffer it takes 256. With a 64 KiB buffer, 16. That is why stdio (the C standard I/O library) buffers `printf` output, why `readv` and `writev` (v for vector, an array of buffers) move several buffers in one call, and why io_uring batches many operations per kernel entry. In io_uring the program and the kernel share two ring buffers, mapped with `mmap`: a submission queue the program fills with I/O requests and a completion queue the kernel fills with results ([io_uring(7)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/io_uring.7.html)).

blocks.title: Mode-switch time to write 1 MiB vs buffer size

scenes.caption: Simplified model: calls = 1 MiB / buffer size, each paying only the FlexSC mode-switch cost. One-byte writes spend 68.4 ms just switching modes; a 4 KiB buffer cuts that 4096 times to 16.7 microseconds.

Raise the per-call cost to 1 microsecond, a stand-in for a call that does real kernel work plus cache refill. The curve shifts up but keeps its slope: every doubling of buffer size halves the call overhead.

blocks.md:
Some calls can skip the kernel entirely. Programs ask for the time constantly, so the kernel maps a tiny shared library, the **vDSO** (virtual dynamic shared object), into every process. On x86-64, [vdso(7)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/vdso.7.html) lists `__vdso_clock_gettime`, `__vdso_gettimeofday`, `__vdso_time` and `__vdso_getcpu`; current kernels also export `__vdso_clock_getres` and `__vdso_getrandom` ([vdso64.lds.S](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/arch/x86/entry/vdso/vdso64/vdso64.lds.S)). glibc calls these instead of issuing a syscall.

The trick: the kernel keeps time data in a page also mapped read-only into your process. The vDSO code reads it inside a retry loop guarded by a sequence counter (if the kernel updated the data mid-read, read again), then adds the elapsed hardware counter ticks. If the clock source cannot be read from user mode, it falls back to a real syscall.

blocks.title: clock_gettime: syscall path vs vDSO path

scenes.caption: Without the vDSO, every clock read is a full syscall: mode switch in, handler, mode switch out.
With the vDSO, glibc makes an ordinary function call into code the kernel mapped into your process. No mode switch.
The kernel updates the shared time data. The vDSO reads it and checks the sequence counter, retrying if an update raced with the read, then adds hardware counter ticks.
If the clock source cannot be read from user mode, the vDSO falls back to the real syscall. Correctness is kept; only speed is lost.

blocks.md: vdso(7) states that calls served by the vDSO do not appear in `strace` output (strace is a tool that prints every system call a process makes) and are invisible to seccomp filters (seccomp, secure computing mode, lets a process restrict which system calls it may make). A trace with zero `clock_gettime` lines does not mean the program never asks for the time.

blocks.prompt: You strace a server that you know calls `clock_gettime` about a million times per second. The trace shows `epoll_wait` (the call that waits for activity on many file descriptors), `read`, `write`, but not a single `clock_gettime`. Bug in strace?
blocks.reveal: No. glibc routes `clock_gettime` to `__vdso_clock_gettime`, which runs entirely in user mode, so there is no system call for strace to intercept. You would see it only if the vDSO fell back to the kernel, for example when the clock source cannot be read from user mode. To count these calls, use a user-space tool such as a uprobe (a kernel tracing hook placed on an instruction in a user program) on the vDSO symbol or a profiler.

blocks.md: A system call is a mode switch plus cache pollution, paid per call. Make fewer, bigger calls (buffering, vectored I/O, batching) and let the vDSO serve the hottest read-only queries without entering the kernel.

blocks.question: A logger issues one `write` per 40-byte log line and handles 200,000 lines per second. Which change cuts syscall overhead the most?
options: Switch from write to pwrite
Accumulate lines in a 64 KiB buffer and write when it fills or on a short timer
Call fsync after every line so the kernel batches better
Open the log file with O_APPEND
blocks.explain: Overhead scales with the number of calls. Buffering 64 KiB packs about 1,638 lines per call, so 200,000 calls per second become about 122. pwrite (write at a given offset) and O_APPEND (every write lands at the end of the file) change semantics, not call count, and fsync, which forces data to disk, adds an even more expensive call per line. Keep a flush timer so a crash or a quiet period does not hold lines forever.

lessons.title: When a system call blocks: sleeping, short counts and EINTR

blocks.md:
So far every call returned at once. Now take a **pipe**, a one-way byte channel the kernel keeps in memory: one process writes into one end and another reads from the other ([pipe(7)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/pipe.7.html)). A program calls `read(p, buf, 16)` on a pipe nobody has written to yet. There is nothing to return, and pipe(7) says the read blocks until data is available.

To **block** means the call does not return yet. Inside the kernel the thread is marked as sleeping and the scheduler runs something else on the CPU: the Blocked state from OS basics. Linux calls the usual kind an *interruptible* sleep (`TASK_INTERRUPTIBLE`), because either the awaited event or a signal can end it ([LWN](https://lwn.net/Articles/288056/)). When a writer adds data, the kernel wakes the reader, which finishes the `read` inside the kernel and returns.

A **signal** is a small asynchronous notice the kernel delivers to a process: SIGALRM when a timer set with `alarm` expires, SIGINT for Ctrl-C, SIGSEGV for an invalid memory access ([signal(7)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/signal.7.html)). Each signal has a default action, often to kill the process. A program can instead install a **handler**, an ordinary function the kernel runs in one of the process's threads when the signal arrives, with [sigaction(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/sigaction.2.html). When the handler returns, the interrupted code carries on.

So what happens to a call that was asleep when the handler ran? signal(7) gives two outcomes: the call is restarted automatically after the handler returns, or it fails with the error `EINTR` (interrupted). Which one depends on the call and on whether the handler was installed with the flag `SA_RESTART`.

blocks.title: A read on an empty pipe, interrupted by SIGALRM

scenes.caption: Two copies of the same program: plain installs the handler without flags, restart with SA_RESTART. Each calls read on an empty pipe and sleeps. A child process will write 2 bytes at t = 2 s; an alarm fires SIGALRM at t = 1 s.
At 1 s SIGALRM arrives. The kernel wakes each sleeping reader and runs its handler. The read has transferred nothing yet.
Without SA_RESTART the read returns -1 with errno EINTR as soon as the handler is done. With SA_RESTART the kernel reissues the same read, which goes back to sleep.
At 2 s the child writes. The restarted read wakes and returns 2 bytes. The program without SA_RESTART returned a second earlier with nothing and must decide for itself whether to retry.

blocks.caption: eintr.c: the program in the figure. Any command-line argument installs the handler with SA_RESTART. The output was produced on macOS, which follows the same POSIX rule as Linux for this case.

blocks.md:
The Linux rules, from signal(7):

- `read`, `write`, `readv` and `writev` on **slow** devices, those that can block for an unbounded time (a terminal, a pipe, a socket), are restarted under `SA_RESTART` and fail with `EINTR` without it. A local disk is not a slow device, so disk I/O is not interrupted by signals.
- Some calls are **never** restarted, whatever the flag: `epoll_wait`, `poll`, `select`, `nanosleep`, `pause`, and socket calls on which a timeout (`SO_RCVTIMEO`) has been set. They always fail with `EINTR`.

The mechanism is visible in the kernel. The pipe code returns an internal code, `ERESTARTSYS`, that programs never see. On the way out to the handler, the x86 signal code ([signal.c](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/arch/x86/kernel/signal.c)) turns it into `-EINTR` unless the handler has `SA_RESTART`; if it does, the code reloads the syscall number into `rax` and moves the saved instruction pointer back 2 bytes, the length of the `syscall` instruction, so the same call runs again.

blocks.code:
read(0, 0x7ffff72cf5cf, 1)              = ? ERESTARTSYS (To be restarted)
--- SIGALRM {si_signo=SIGALRM, si_code=SI_KERNEL} ---
rt_sigreturn({mask=[]})                 = 0
read(0, "", 1)                          = 0
blocks.caption: Example output printed in strace(1): a read interrupted by SIGALRM and then restarted. rt_sigreturn is the system call that ends a handler and resumes the interrupted code (sigreturn(2)).

blocks.md:
The second surprise is the **short count**. `read` and `write` return how many bytes they actually moved, which may be fewer than you asked for. [read(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/read.2.html) says this is not an error: fewer bytes may be available right now (near end of file, or from a pipe or terminal), or the call was interrupted by a signal. [write(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/write.2.html) lists the same signal case. The kernel's pipe code ([fs/pipe.c](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/fs/pipe.c)) shows the exact rule for a blocking write: copy what fits, sleep until a reader makes room, and if a signal is pending, return the count already copied. Only when nothing was copied does the call become `EINTR` or a restart.

A pipe holds 65,536 bytes by default on Linux (16 pages of 4 KiB, per pipe(7)), so a large write to a busy pipe is exactly where this happens.

blocks.title: write_all: a 10,000-byte write into a nearly full pipe

scenes.caption: Simplified model: the pipe holds 65,536 bytes and already has 59,536 queued, so 6,000 bytes are free. We must write 10,000 bytes, and SIGALRM fires now and then (handler without SA_RESTART).
Call 1: write(fd, buf, 10000). The kernel copies the 6,000 bytes that fit, then sleeps waiting for room. A SIGALRM arrives; bytes were already copied, so write returns 6000, a short count.
No error, so advance: done = 6000. A single write() would have silently dropped the last 4,000 bytes here.
Call 2: write(fd, buf + 6000, 4000). The pipe is still full, so the call sleeps at once; another SIGALRM arrives before a single byte is copied. Result: -1 with errno EINTR. Retry.
Call 3: the reader has drained the pipe, so all 4,000 remaining bytes fit. write returns 4000 and done reaches 10000.
Three write calls for one logical write: 6,000 + EINTR + 4,000. The exact pattern depends on timing, but the loop is correct for every pattern.

blocks.caption: A real run of write_all: 1 MiB into a pipe drained by a slow child, while an interval timer (setitimer) sends SIGALRM every millisecond. Includes and the counter variables are omitted. Counts vary from run to run; every run delivered all 1,048,576 bytes.

blocks.md: The third case is a **non-blocking** descriptor. With the `O_NONBLOCK` flag set (via `fcntl`), a call that would have to sleep fails at once with `EAGAIN`; for sockets the error may be `EWOULDBLOCK`, and read(2) says to check both. Event loops rely on this: they ask the kernel which descriptors are ready (with `epoll_wait`) and then read until `EAGAIN`. Non-blocking writes are short too: pipe(7) says a non-blocking write of more than `PIPE_BUF` bytes (4096 on Linux) to a pipe with some free room writes from 1 to n bytes.

Retrying `EINTR` is right for `read` and `write`. For calls with a timeout (`poll`, `epoll_wait`, `nanosleep`), retrying with the original timeout restarts the clock, so a steady stream of signals could stretch the wait without limit. Recompute the time left before retrying.

Every `read` and `write` may block, move fewer bytes than asked, or fail with `EINTR` or `EAGAIN`. Loop until all bytes are moved, retry on `EINTR`, and treat `EAGAIN` as "wait until the descriptor is ready".

blocks.question: A server sends a 1 MB response with `if (write(sock, buf, 1000000) == -1) die();` on a non-blocking socket. Clients sometimes receive truncated responses but the server logs no error. Why?
options: The kernel splits large writes into packets and some packets are lost
write returned -1 with EAGAIN, which die() ignored
write returned a short count, fewer than 1,000,000 bytes, and the code never sent the rest
Sockets need fsync before the data is sent
blocks.explain: A non-blocking socket accepts only what fits in its send buffer and returns that count. The check only catches -1, so the rest of the buffer is silently never sent. The fix is a write_all style loop that advances by the returned count and waits for writability (for example with epoll) on EAGAIN. TCP itself retransmits lost packets, so loss is not the cause.

blocks.question: A handler for SIGCHLD is installed with SA_RESTART. Which blocked call can still fail with EINTR when SIGCHLD arrives?
options: read on a pipe
epoll_wait
waitpid
write on a socket with no timeout set
blocks.explain: signal(7) lists epoll_wait, poll and select among the calls that are never restarted, regardless of SA_RESTART. read and write on pipes and sockets, and waitpid, are restarted when the handler has SA_RESTART. Event loops therefore always check for EINTR after epoll_wait.

lessons.title: mmap: putting a file into your address space

blocks.md:
To process a file with `read`, you copy chunks from the kernel into a buffer you own, one syscall per chunk, and you manage offsets yourself. `mmap` offers a different deal: ask the kernel once to make a range of your virtual address space *stand for* the file, then use plain pointers. Byte `i` of the file is just `p[i]`.

The call is `mmap(addr, length, prot, flags, fd, offset)`. `addr` is usually `NULL` so the kernel picks a page-aligned address. `prot` is `PROT_NONE` (no access at all) or a bitwise OR of `PROT_READ`, `PROT_WRITE` and `PROT_EXEC`. `flags` must include exactly one of `MAP_SHARED`, `MAP_PRIVATE` or `MAP_SHARED_VALIDATE` (a stricter `MAP_SHARED` that rejects flags the kernel does not recognize); the MAP_SHARED lesson covers them. `fd` and `offset` say which file bytes back the range.

blocks.caption: Sum every byte of a file through a read-only mapping. fstat fills in the file's metadata, including its size. Error checks on open and fstat omitted for brevity.

blocks.md: The surprising part is what `mmap` does *not* do. It reserves the address range and records which file and offset back it, as one new **virtual memory area** (VMA, one line of `/proc/PID/maps` from the virtual memory course), but it reads nothing from disk and fills no page table entries. The work happens later, one page at a time: the first touch of each page raises a **page fault**, the kernel finds the file data (reading it from disk into the page cache, the kernel's in-memory copy of file pages, if needed), installs a page table entry, and restarts the instruction. This is demand paging (filling each page only when it is first touched), which you met in the virtual memory course, now backed by a file instead of zero-filled anonymous memory.

blocks.caption: With 4 KiB pages, byte 5000 is in page 1 at offset 904, because 5000 = 4096 + 904. Since 4096 is 2 to the 12th, the page is i shifted right by 12 bits (i >> 12) and the offset is its low 12 bits, i AND 4095 (i & 4095).

blocks.title: A 10,000-byte file mapped with length 16,384

scenes.caption: mmap returned. 16,384 bytes of address space (4 pages) are reserved, but nothing is resident. The file has 10,000 bytes: two full pages, 1,808 bytes in page 2, none in page 3.
Read p[0]. No page table entry exists, so the CPU faults. The kernel reads page 0 of the file into the page cache (a major fault, since it needed I/O) and maps it.

Read p[5000]: page 1, offset 904. Simplified: one fault per page. On Linux, read-ahead and fault-around (the strace lesson) often bring in and map neighbouring pages at once, so this touch may cost a minor fault or none.
Read p[11000]: page 2, offset 2808, past the file's 1,808 bytes in that page. This page faults in like the others, but its bytes past end of file are zero-filled, so the read returns 0. No error.
Read p[13000]: page 3 lies wholly beyond the end of the file. The kernel delivers SIGBUS (bus error: the address is mapped but nothing backs it), which kills the process unless it is handled.

blocks.md:
The rules from [mmap(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/mmap.2.html), all visible above:

- `offset` must be a multiple of the page size (`sysconf(_SC_PAGE_SIZE)`), otherwise the call fails with `EINVAL` (invalid argument). `length` need not be; the mapping covers whole pages.
- In the last partial page, bytes past end of file read as zero, and writes there are never carried to the file.
- Touching a page entirely beyond end of file raises `SIGBUS`. Writing to a read-only mapping raises `SIGSEGV`. Both are signals: unless a handler is installed, as in the blocking lesson, they kill the process.
- You may `close(fd)` right after `mmap`; the mapping keeps the file referenced.
- The kernel reports faults it served from memory and from disk separately, as minor and major faults in [getrusage(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/getrusage.2.html).
`mmap` signals failure with `MAP_FAILED`, which is `(void *) -1`, not `NULL`. Code that checks `if (p == NULL)` misses every error and later dereferences address -1.
mmap is lazy. The call sets up a promise; each page is paid for with a page fault on first touch. Errors that `read` would return as a value (file truncated, disk error) arrive as signals instead.

blocks.question: You want to map a file starting at byte 5000. Page size is 4096. What do you pass, and where is byte 5000 in the result?
options: offset 5000; byte 5000 is at p[0]
offset 0; byte 5000 is at p[904]
offset 8192; byte 5000 is at p[-3192]
offset 4096; byte 5000 is at p[904]
blocks.explain: offset must be page-aligned, so round 5000 down to 4096 and add the remainder yourself: 5000 - 4096 = 904. Passing 5000 fails with EINVAL. Remember to extend length by the same 904 bytes so the end of the range you want is still covered.

blocks.question: The 10,000-byte file is mapped writable with MAP_SHARED and length 12,288. You write p[10500] = 'x'. What happens?
options: SIGBUS, because byte 10,500 is past end of file
The file grows to 10,501 bytes
The write succeeds in memory but is never written to the file
SIGSEGV, because shared mappings cannot be written past EOF
blocks.explain: Byte 10,500 is in page 2, the last partial page, so it is mapped and zero-filled. mmap(2) says modifications to that tail region are not written out to the file. mmap never changes a file's size; use ftruncate first if you need the file to grow. SIGBUS would only come from touching page 3, which is wholly beyond EOF.

lessons.title: Editing the map: munmap, mprotect, mremap and how exec builds it

blocks.md:
The virtual memory course showed `/proc/PID/maps`: one line per **virtual memory area** (VMA), a run of addresses with one set of permissions and one backing. The `mmap` call from the last lesson adds exactly one VMA to that list. It records start, end, permissions, flags, and the file and offset behind the range, and nothing else happens until a page is touched.

This lesson covers the calls that edit the list after that (`munmap`, `mprotect`, `mremap`) and the `mmap` calls that run before your `main` even starts. Remember the page size: on x86-64 Linux, 4 KiB.

Who makes the first VMAs? `execve`, the system call that starts a new program. LWN's walk through the kernel's ELF loader ([How programs get run: ELF binaries](https://lwn.net/Articles/631631/)) gives the steps. **ELF** (Executable and Linkable Format) is the file format of Linux programs; its *program header table* lists **segments**. The kernel cares about `PT_LOAD` segments, which describe the program's memory (code and data, plus the size of the zero-filled bss), and `PT_INTERP`, which names the run-time linker.

The kernel sets up the stack, maps each `PT_LOAD` segment, sets up zero-filled pages for the bss, and maps the vDSO pages. For a dynamically linked program it also maps the interpreter's own `PT_LOAD` segments (typically `/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2`) and starts execution there, not at your code. The run-time linker, ld.so, then finds each shared library, maps it with `mmap`, resolves symbols, and only then jumps to the program's entry point.

blocks.title: How execve and ld.so build the first VMAs

scenes.caption: execve opens the file and reads its ELF header and program header table. The old program's VMAs are thrown away.
Each PT_LOAD segment becomes a file-backed VMA (code r-x, read-only data r--, data rw-), with zero-filled pages for the bss after the data.
The kernel also places the stack (at a randomized top) and maps the vDSO pages from the cost lesson.
PT_INTERP names the run-time linker. The kernel maps its PT_LOAD segments too and sets the start address to the interpreter's entry point, not the program's.
ld.so runs in user mode. It finds the shared libraries the program needs and maps each one with ordinary mmap calls, so every library adds a few more VMAs.
With symbols resolved, ld.so jumps to the program's own entry point, and eventually main runs. All of this happened before your first line of code.

blocks.md:
Three calls edit the list afterwards. All take page-aligned addresses and work on whole pages.

- **munmap(addr, len)** removes the pages: [mmap(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/mmap.2.html) says later references to them generate SIGSEGV. Unmapping the middle of a VMA leaves two smaller VMAs, one on each side.
- **mprotect(addr, len, prot)** changes permissions ([mprotect(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/mprotect.2.html)); an access that breaks them gets SIGSEGV. A VMA has one set of permissions, so the man page's own example: making the middle of a read/write region read-only results in three mappings.
- **mremap(old, old_len, new_len, flags)** grows, shrinks or moves a mapping ([mremap(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/mremap.2.html)). If there is no room to grow in place it fails, unless `MREMAP_MAYMOVE` lets the kernel move it; then every pointer into the old range is invalid. The man page notes this makes a very efficient `realloc`: the kernel moves page table entries instead of copying bytes.

blocks.title: Four anonymous pages, edited twice

scenes.caption: Before: nothing is mapped at these four page addresses.
mmap 4 pages read/write, private anonymous. One VMA, one line in /proc/self/maps. No physical page exists yet.
mprotect page 2 to PROT_READ. One VMA cannot hold two permission sets, so the kernel splits A into three: pages 0 to 1, page 2, page 3. Count: 3 VMAs.
munmap page 1. The first piece shrinks to page 0 and a hole opens. Still 3 VMAs: page 0, page 2, page 3.
Accesses now: page 0 read or write works, page 1 anything faults (no VMA), page 2 reads work but writes fault (permissions), page 3 works.

blocks.caption: What /proc/self/maps would show after each step on x86-64 Linux, built from the rules in proc_pid_maps(5). The addresses are illustrative, and in a real process the kernel may merge a new anonymous mapping with a neighbour that has the same attributes.

blocks.prompt: After those two edits the program tries five accesses: read page 0, write page 1, read page 2, write page 2, write page 3. Which ones fault?
blocks.reveal: **Write page 1** faults because no VMA covers it any more, and **write page 2** faults because the VMA is read-only. The others succeed: page 0 and page 3 are still read/write, and page 2 can be read. On Linux both faults are SIGSEGV (mmap(2) for unmapped pages, mprotect(2) for a protection violation). The run below catches the signals with a handler and `siglongjmp` (a jump back to a saved point in the program) so it can keep going.

blocks.caption: vma.c: the same edits and accesses, using the system page size. On macOS the protection fault is delivered as SIGBUS, a macOS difference; Linux delivers SIGSEGV for both faults.

blocks.md: Each VMA costs kernel memory, so the number per process is capped by `vm.max_map_count`, default 65,530 ([sysctl vm docs](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/sysctl/vm.html)); some distributions raise it, Fedora to 1,048,576 since Fedora 39. The docs say most programs need fewer than a thousand, and malloc debuggers may use one or two per allocation. Worked example: a debugging allocator puts a `PROT_NONE` guard page after every block. Each block then needs 2 VMAs (data, guard), so the cap is reached at about 65,530 / 2 = 32,765 live blocks (a few fewer, since the program's code, libraries, heap and stack already use some VMAs), and the next `mmap` or `mprotect` fails with `ENOMEM`.

`munmap` can fail with `ENOMEM` even though it frees memory. mmap(2) explains why: unmapping a region in the middle of a mapping creates two smaller mappings, and that can exceed the per-process limit.

The kernel's view of your memory is a list of VMAs. `execve` and ld.so create the first ones, `mmap` adds, `munmap` removes and splits, `mprotect` splits by permission, and `mremap` resizes or moves. `/proc/PID/maps` is that list, and it is the first thing to read when a mapping misbehaves.

blocks.question: A 3-page read/write anonymous mapping has its middle page changed to PROT_READ, and then its last page unmapped. How many lines does this region now take in /proc/self/maps?
blocks.explain: mprotect splits the region into three VMAs (rw, r, rw). munmap of the last page removes the third VMA entirely, leaving page 0 (rw) and page 1 (r): 2 lines. No hole is created inside a remaining VMA, so nothing else splits.

blocks.question: A program grows a 1 GiB mapping with mremap(p, 1 GiB, 2 GiB, MREMAP_MAYMOVE) and keeps using a pointer it saved earlier, q = p + 4096. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing: mremap always grows a mapping in place
If the kernel moved the mapping, q points into the old, now unmapped range, so using it can fault
The first 1 GiB is copied byte by byte, so q sees stale data
mremap fails because MREMAP_MAYMOVE only works on file mappings
blocks.explain: With MREMAP_MAYMOVE the kernel may relocate the mapping when there is no room to grow in place, and mremap(2) warns that absolute pointers into the old location become invalid. Use the returned address, or store offsets from the start instead of raw pointers.

blocks.md: Where do the bytes behind a file mapping live? In the **page cache**: the kernel's in-memory copy of file pages, shared by everyone using that file. `read` copies bytes out of a page cache page into your buffer. A file mapping instead points your page table entry *at the page cache page itself*. No copy, and no syscall per access. The saving is concrete: reading a 100 MiB file through a 4 KiB buffer takes 25,600 `read` calls, each copying 4 KiB from the page cache page into your buffer, 100 MiB of copying in all; the mapping copies nothing, which is exactly the benefit database developers were after (Crotty, Leis and Pavlo, in a paper at CIDR 2022, the Conference on Innovative Data Systems Research).

blocks.title: First and second touch of a mapped page

scenes.caption: A loads from a mapped address. The MMU finds no valid page table entry and raises a page fault into the kernel.
The kernel finds which file and offset back this address. The page is not in the page cache, so it must read the disk: a major fault.
The kernel installs a page table entry pointing at the page cache page and returns. The CPU retries the same load, which now succeeds.
Process B maps the same file and touches the same page. It still faults (its own page table is empty), but the data is already cached: a minor fault, no disk I/O.

blocks.md:
The flags decide what happens on a **write**:

- `MAP_SHARED`: writes go to the shared page cache page. Other processes mapping the same region see them, and the kernel eventually writes them to the file. A page changed in memory but not yet written back to its file is called **dirty**.
- `MAP_PRIVATE`: a private **copy-on-write** mapping. Reads share the page cache page, but the first write to a page makes the kernel copy it into a fresh page that only this process sees. The file never changes. The kernel's page fault code has names for these cases: `do_read_fault`, `do_shared_fault`, `do_cow_fault`.

blocks.title: One file page, a shared mapper and a private mapper

scenes.caption: Both processes read the page. Their page table entries point at the same physical page cache page. One copy of the data in RAM.
A writes through its MAP_SHARED mapping. The page cache page changes in place and is marked dirty. Any other MAP_SHARED mapper sees the new bytes immediately.
Whether B, a MAP_PRIVATE mapper that has not written this page, sees A's change is unspecified by mmap(2). Do not rely on it either way.
B writes. Its entry was read-only, so the write faults; the kernel copies the page into a new private page and repoints B there. A and the file never see B's change.
The kernel writes A's dirty page to disk at a time of its choosing, or when A calls msync. B's private copy is never written to the file.

blocks.md: When do `MAP_SHARED` writes reach the disk? [msync(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/msync.2.html) says that without `msync` there is no guarantee they are written back before `munmap`. `MS_SYNC` requests the write and waits for it; `MS_ASYNC` schedules it and returns (on Linux it is a no-op, since the kernel already tracks dirty pages). The kernel is also free to write dirty pages back earlier on its own, which matters for databases (the last lesson). Databases cope with a **write-ahead log** (each change is first appended to a separate log file and forced to disk, so after a crash it can be replayed or undone) or with **shadow paging** (changed pages are written to fresh locations, and one root pointer is switched to them only once they are on disk). LMDB, the Lightning Memory-Mapped Database, uses the second.

Take one transaction that changes two pages, A and B. The write-ahead rule, in PostgreSQL's words, is that changes to data files must be written only after the log records describing them have been flushed to permanent storage ([WAL introduction](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/wal-intro.html)). Then a crash at any moment is recoverable: committed changes can be redone from the log.

`MAP_SHARED` breaks the order. If the database edits page A in place through a shared mapping, A is dirty in the page cache, and the kernel may write it to the file before the log record is on disk. Crotty, Leis and Pavlo put it this way: the OS can flush a dirty page at any time, whether or not the transaction has committed, and the database gets no warning. So mmap-based designs stage changes elsewhere: MongoDB's MMAPv1 engine wrote into a `MAP_PRIVATE` copy and logged changes, and LMDB uses shadow paging: copy A and B to free pages, flush them (`msync` with a writable map; LMDB's default uses write calls and a sync), then switch the root pointer. LMDB allows only one writer at a time.

blocks.title: A two-page update: what reaches disk, and when

scenes.caption: WAL done right (time in arbitrary steps). The log records for A and B are appended and fsynced first; the transaction commits at step 3. Data pages are written later, in any order.
Editing in place through MAP_SHARED: the kernel's writeback picks dirty page A at step 1, before the log is on disk. A crash at step 2 leaves new A, old B and no log record to undo A.
Shadow paging (LMDB style): copies of A and B go to free pages and are msynced. The old root still points at the old A and B, so a crash here loses nothing committed.
Commit is a single small write: switch the root pointer to the new pages, then msync. Before the switch a reader sees old A and B; after it, new A' and B'. Never a mix.

blocks.md: `MAP_ANONYMOUS` mappings have no file at all: pages start zero-filled. That is how allocators get large blocks. glibc `malloc` uses `mmap` for requests at or above `M_MMAP_THRESHOLD`, which starts at 128 KiB and adjusts upward dynamically as large blocks are freed ([mallopt(3)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/mallopt.3.html)). Freeing such a block returns it to the kernel with `munmap`.

As the virtual memory course showed, copy-on-write is also how `fork` stays cheap: the child gets copies of the parent's page tables, both point at the same physical pages, and a page is duplicated only when one side writes it ([fork(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/fork.2.html)). A worked example with 4 KiB pages: a parent holding 1 GiB of written anonymous memory has 262,144 pages. Right after `fork`, physical use is still 262,144 pages. If the child then writes a quarter of them, 65,536 pages are copied.

blocks.title: Physical 4 KiB pages: 1 GiB process forks

scenes.caption: Before fork: the parent owns all 262,144 pages.
Right after fork: nothing is copied. All 262,144 pages are shared, marked read-only in both page tables.
The child writes 25% of the pages (65,536). Each write faults and copies one page. Total physical pages: 196,608 + 65,536 + 65,536 = 327,680, or 1.25 GiB.

blocks.question: Two worker processes map the same data file. Worker 1 uses MAP_SHARED and writes a record. Worker 2 uses MAP_PRIVATE and has only read that page. Which statement is guaranteed?
options: Worker 2 sees the new record immediately
Worker 2 never sees the new record
Whether worker 2 sees it is unspecified, so code must not depend on it
The write fails because a private mapping of the page exists
blocks.explain: mmap(2) states it is unspecified whether changes made to the file after the mmap call are visible in a MAP_PRIVATE mapping. In practice an untouched private page often still points at the page cache page, but once worker 2 writes that page it has its own copy. Use MAP_SHARED in both if they must see each other's writes.

blocks.question: A program writes 100 MB into a MAP_SHARED file mapping, then the machine loses power before the program calls msync or munmap. What can you say about the file?
options: None of the writes are in the file
All of the writes are in the file, because shared mappings write through
The file is restored from the page cache on reboot
Any subset of the dirty pages may have reached the file
blocks.explain: The kernel writes dirty pages back whenever it chooses, so some may have reached the disk and others not, in no order you control. msync with MS_SYNC is how you force a range to disk and wait. This lack of ordering is why mmap-based databases still need a write-ahead log or shadow paging (as LMDB uses) to stay consistent.

lessons.title: Shared memory between processes: MAP_SHARED, shm_open and memfd

blocks.md:
A parent wants a counter its child can update. An ordinary variable will not do: after `fork` the child's writes go to its own copy-on-write pages, as the last lesson showed, and the parent never sees them. The same is true of a `MAP_PRIVATE` mapping.

The fix is one flag. mmap(2) says memory mapped by `mmap` is preserved across `fork` with the same attributes, and that `MAP_SHARED` updates are visible to other processes mapping the same region. So map the counter with `MAP_SHARED | MAP_ANONYMOUS` *before* forking: both page tables then point at the same physical page, and a store by either process is a store to that page. This is **shared memory**, the fastest way for processes to exchange data: no system call per message, no copy.

blocks.title: Three ways to put the same pages in two processes

nodes.label:
memfd_create
fd passed over
a UNIX socket

scenes.caption: The goal: page table entries in two processes that point at the same physical pages. Then a store by A is immediately a load result for B.
Related processes: map MAP_SHARED | MAP_ANONYMOUS, then fork. The child inherits the mapping with the same attributes, so it shares the pages instead of copying them.

Unrelated processes, by name: shm_open creates an object in a memory-only file system (tmpfs, usually at /dev/shm). Each process opens the same name, sets its size with ftruncate, and maps it MAP_SHARED.

Without any name: memfd_create returns a descriptor for an anonymous file in RAM. Pass it on (inherit it across fork, or send it over a UNIX domain socket, a local socket that can carry descriptors) and both map it.

blocks.md:
The two named and descriptor-based routes in more detail:

- **POSIX shared memory** ([shm_overview(7)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/shm_overview.7.html)): `shm_open` creates or opens an object and returns a file descriptor, much like `open`. A new object has length zero, so set its size with `ftruncate`, then `mmap` it. On Linux the objects live in a tmpfs file system, normally mounted at `/dev/shm`, and they persist until the system shuts down or until every process has unmapped the object and it has been removed with `shm_unlink`.
- **memfd** ([memfd_create(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/memfd_create.2.html)): creates an anonymous file that lives in RAM and is freed when the last reference goes away. It also starts at size zero. The man page lists three ways to give it to a second process: inherit it across `fork`, send the descriptor over a UNIX domain socket, or open `/proc/PID/fd/N`.

Sharing pages shares bytes, nothing more. shm_overview(7) says processes typically must synchronize access, for example with POSIX semaphores. The danger is subtle: the compiler and the CPU may reorder ordinary loads and stores, so another process can see a "message ready" flag before it sees the message.

C11 atomics fix this with ordering rules ([memory_order](https://en.cppreference.com/w/c/atomic/memory_order)). A **release** store publishes: every write before it in this thread becomes visible to a thread that does an **acquire** load of the same variable and reads the stored value. On x86 the hardware already gives release and acquire ordering for most operations, so they only stop compiler reordering; on ARM they emit special instructions. Do processes count as threads here? The C++ standard recommends (but does not require) that lock-free atomics also be *address-free*, usable between processes through shared memory ([is_lock_free](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/atomic/atomic/is_lock_free)). The ring below relies on that, so check `atomic_is_lock_free` on your platform.

blocks.title: An 8-slot ring buffer in a shared page, 10 messages

scenes.caption: One shared page holds head (next slot to write), tail (next slot to read) and 8 slots. Both start at 0, so the ring is empty: head equals tail.
The producer writes 100, 200, ..., 800 into slots 0 to 7, each followed by a release store of head. head = 8, tail = 0: head minus tail is 8, so the ring is full and the producer spins.
The consumer acquire-loads head, sees 8, and reads slots 0, 1 and 2 (100, 200, 300), release-storing tail after each read (1, then 2, then 3). Three slots are free again.
The producer writes into slot head mod 8: with head 8 the 9th message (900) lands in slot 0, with head 9 the 10th (1000) lands in slot 1. head = 10.

The consumer drains the rest: 400 to 800, then 900 and 1000. tail = 10 = head, empty again. Sum: 100 + 200 + ... + 1000 = 5,500. This is one possible interleaving; the code is correct for all of them.

blocks.caption: ring.c: a single-producer, single-consumer ring in a MAP_SHARED | MAP_ANONYMOUS page shared across fork. The slot write is a plain store; the release store of head publishes it.

blocks.prompt: Suppose `head` and `tail` were plain `unsigned` instead of `_Atomic`, with the same logic. What could go wrong?
blocks.reveal: Two things. The compiler may keep `head` in a register inside `while (head == t) ;`, so the consumer spins forever on a stale copy. And the compiler (or, on ARM, the CPU) may make the store to `head` visible before the store to the slot, so the consumer reads a slot that does not hold the message yet. The release store on `head` and the acquire load in the consumer forbid exactly that reordering.

blocks.md: No `msync` appears anywhere, and none is needed. `msync` is about the *file*: it controls when changes are written back to the backing file. Visibility between processes is immediate because they share physical pages, whether the pages are anonymous, in `/dev/shm` or in a memfd. A `MAP_SHARED` mapping of a regular file is also a shared region, one whose contents outlive the processes; making those writes durable on disk is where `msync` comes back in.

The ring spins while it waits, burning a whole CPU. Real shared-memory queues sleep when empty or full, for example on a POSIX semaphore placed in the shared region, as shm_overview(7) suggests, and use spinning at most for a short time first.

To share writable memory, both processes need `MAP_SHARED` mappings of the same pages: anonymous before `fork`, a `shm_open` name, or a memfd descriptor. Then order the accesses with release and acquire atomics or a lock; the mapping itself guarantees no ordering at all.

blocks.question: A parent wants to read a result its child writes after fork. Which setup makes the child's write visible to the parent?
options: malloc a buffer before fork
mmap with MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANONYMOUS before fork
mmap with MAP_SHARED | MAP_ANONYMOUS in the child after fork
mmap with MAP_SHARED | MAP_ANONYMOUS before fork
blocks.explain: Only a shared mapping that exists before fork is inherited by the child with the same attributes, so both point at the same pages. malloc memory and MAP_PRIVATE mappings are copy-on-write after fork, so the child's write lands in its own copy. A mapping created in the child after fork exists only in the child.

blocks.question: Two unrelated programs, a camera daemon and a viewer, must share a 64 MiB frame buffer. The daemon should not leave a name in /dev/shm that another user could open. Which approach fits?
options: memfd_create in the daemon, then send the descriptor to the viewer over a UNIX domain socket
MAP_SHARED | MAP_ANONYMOUS in the daemon; the viewer maps the same address
shm_open with a random name, never unlinked
Write frames to a pipe; pipes are shared memory
blocks.explain: A memfd has no name in any file system; only processes holding the descriptor can map it, and memfd_create(2) lists passing it over a UNIX domain socket as one way to share it. An anonymous mapping is reachable only through fork. A shm_open name is visible in /dev/shm until unlinked. A pipe copies every byte through the kernel.

lessons.title: Watching and restricting system calls: strace, faults and seccomp

blocks.md:
This lesson turns the numbers from earlier lessons into things you can observe. The main tool is **strace**, which, in its manual's words, intercepts and records the system calls made by a process and the signals it receives ([strace(1)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/strace.1.html)). Each line shows the call's name, its arguments and its return value; errors show -1 with the errno name, as in `open("/foo/bar", O_RDONLY) = -1 ENOENT`. strace is built on ptrace, the kernel's debugging interface, and its manual warns that a traced process runs more slowly.

Four options cover most uses:

- `-c`: count calls, errors and time per system call and print a summary table at exit.
- `-T`: show the time spent in each call.
- `-f`: follow child processes and threads.
- `-e trace=%memory`: show only memory mapping calls (`mmap`, `munmap`, `mprotect`, `brk` and relatives).

blocks.caption: sumread.c: the read() twin of the byte-summing program from the mmap lesson, with a 4 KiB buffer. It needs Linux, so no output is shown here; predict it first.

blocks.prompt: Predict the `strace -c` row for `read` in sumread on the 100 MiB file, and how many calls the mmap version makes to touch the same data.
blocks.reveal: **read: about 25,601 calls.** 104,857,600 / 4,096 = 25,600 calls that return data, plus one that returns 0 at end of file, plus a startup read or two (ld.so reads the first 832 bytes of libc with `read`). The mmap version makes a handful: `openat`, `fstat`, `mmap`, `close`, `munmap` (plus the startup calls both programs share). Its cost did not vanish; it moved into page faults, which strace does not show.

blocks.md:
Page faults are counted by [getrusage(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/getrusage.2.html): `ru_minflt` for faults served without I/O and `ru_majflt` for faults that needed I/O. With 4 KiB pages one might expect 25,600 faults for the mapping. With the file already in the page cache, expect about 16 times fewer: on a read fault of a file mapping, Linux also maps cached neighbours, up to 64 KiB around the address (`fault_around_pages` in [mm/memory.c](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/mm/memory.c)), so 25,600 / 16 = 1,600 minor faults. With a cold cache, read-ahead makes the major faults far fewer than one per page as well.

The read version pays something the mmap version does not: every byte is copied from the page cache into `buf` (in `filemap_read`, [mm/filemap.c](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/mm/filemap.c)), 100 MiB of copying in total.

blocks.title: Kernel entries to sum a 100 MiB cached file (model)

scenes.caption: Predicted read calls: 25,601 with a 4 KiB buffer, 1,601 with 64 KiB (100 MiB / 64 KiB = 1,600, plus the final 0). These are model predictions, not measurements.

Add the mmap version's page faults: about 1,600 minor faults with fault-around mapping 16 cached pages per fault. Fewer kernel entries than 4 KiB reads, no copy, but each entry is a fault rather than a call.

blocks.md: Trust strace's counts more than its times. Tracing stops the program at every call, so `-c` and `-T` times are inflated, and calls served by the vDSO never appear at all (the cost lesson). Measure speed without strace, for example with `perf stat`, and use strace to learn what the program does.

blocks.caption: alloc.c: watch glibc malloc switch from the heap to mmap at M_MMAP_THRESHOLD (128 KiB by default, from the MAP_SHARED lesson). Loader startup also prints mmap lines for the libraries, as in the lesson on editing the map.

blocks.md:
Seeing system calls is half the story; the other half is restricting them. **seccomp** (secure computing mode) lets a thread give up system calls for good ([seccomp(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/seccomp.2.html)):

- **Strict mode** allows only `read`, `write`, `_exit` (but not `exit_group`) and `sigreturn`. Any other call kills the thread, or the whole process with SIGKILL when it has one thread.
- **Filter mode** runs a small BPF program (Berkeley Packet Filter, a tiny in-kernel bytecode) on every system call. The filter sees the architecture, the syscall number and the arguments, and returns an action: `SECCOMP_RET_ALLOW`, `SECCOMP_RET_ERRNO` (fail with a chosen errno without running the call), `SECCOMP_RET_KILL_PROCESS`, and others.

An unprivileged thread must first set the `no_new_privs` bit with `prctl(PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS, 1)`. Filters are inherited by children and kept across `execve`, so a launcher can sandbox the program it starts.

blocks.title: Where a seccomp filter sits

scenes.caption: Every system call enters the kernel through the same entry path. With a filter installed, the kernel runs it before dispatching the call.
write is on the allow list: the filter returns ALLOW and the normal handler runs.
getpid is not on the list: the filter returns ERRNO with EPERM. The handler never runs; the program sees -1 and errno EPERM.
A call from an unexpected architecture (a 32-bit entry, say) hits the KILL action, so the process dies at once.
clock_gettime served by the vDSO never enters the kernel, so the filter never sees it. seccomp(2) states this caveat directly.

blocks.caption: filter.c: allow read, write and exit_group, fail everything else with EPERM, and kill on a foreign architecture. Linux x86-64 only; not run here. The layout follows the example program in seccomp(2).

blocks.reveal: Most likely `getpid=-1 errno=1 clock=0`. getpid is filtered, so it returns -1 with errno 1 (`EPERM`). clock_gettime is served by the vDSO in user mode and succeeds even though it is not on the allow list; seccomp(2) notes the vDSO can fall back to the real system call in some cases, and then the filter would block it. `snprintf` needs no system call, `write` is allowed, and returning from main calls `exit_group`, which is allowed too.

blocks.md: Filters match system call **numbers**, and seccomp(2) warns that C library wrappers do not always use the call their name suggests. `exit` uses `exit_group`, `fork` uses `clone`, and since glibc 2.26 `open` uses `openat`. That is also why strict mode is awkward: returning from `main` calls `exit_group`, which strict mode does not allow, so a strict-mode program must end with a raw `syscall(SYS_exit, 0)`.

blocks.caption: strict.c: strict mode. The write succeeds; ending with exit_group (a normal return from main) would get the process killed. Linux only; not run here.

blocks.md: strace shows which calls a program makes and how often; getrusage shows the page faults that strace cannot see; seccomp turns a list of needed calls into an enforced allow-list. All three work on syscall numbers and miss the vDSO.

blocks.question: A sandbox's seccomp allow-list includes SYS_open, SYS_read, SYS_write and SYS_exit_group. A program inside calls fopen("data.txt", "r") and gets EPERM. Why?
options: fopen needs SYS_close on the list before it can open
glibc's open wrapper has used the openat system call since glibc 2.26, and openat is not on the list
Filters cannot allow file system calls
fopen is served by the vDSO
blocks.explain: seccomp filters match the system call number the kernel sees, and seccomp(2) notes that glibc switched open to openat in 2.26. Strace the program to find the calls it really makes, then build the list from that.

blocks.question: strace -c on a busy program shows 2 million read calls taking 4 s of system time. Without strace, the program's total run time is 1.5 s. What is the best reading?
options: The program spends 4 s in read; strace measures it exactly
strace double-counts calls made by threads
read must be served by the vDSO in the untraced run
The call count is trustworthy, but strace's own overhead inflates the times, so measure time without it
blocks.explain: Tracing stops the program around every call, so times under strace are inflated; strace(1) warns that a traced process runs more slowly. The count of 2 million is what the program really does, and it suggests a bigger buffer. read has no vDSO version.

lessons.title: When mmap wins, when it hurts, and how to steer it

blocks.md: mmap shines when data is read often, fits comfortably in memory, and is shared. Executables and shared libraries are mapped this way; the kernel's own documentation for `max_map_count` (default 65530 mappings per process) says mappings come from malloc, direct mmap, mprotect and madvise calls, and loading shared libraries. Read-mostly lookup tables and indexes loaded by several processes get one copy in the page cache, with no copy into each process and no syscall per access. LMDB relies on mmap entirely, and SQLite offers it as an option.

It hurts when the data is much larger than memory and the program needs control. The usual alternative in a database is a **buffer pool**: its own in-memory cache of file pages, filled with explicit reads, where the database decides which pages to evict and when each one is written. While a transaction is using a page, the buffer pool **pins** it, marking it as not to be evicted or written yet.

Crotty, Leis and Pavlo ("Are You Sure You Want to Use MMAP in Your Database Management System?", CIDR 2022) list four problems:

1. **Transactional safety**: the OS can write a dirty page to the file at any moment, even a pinned one, so a half-finished transaction can reach disk.
2. **I/O stalls**: any pointer dereference can block on a disk read, and there is no asynchronous way to fault a page in.
3. **Error handling**: an I/O error arrives as `SIGBUS` at whatever instruction touched the page, not as a return value.
4. **Performance**: page table contention, single-threaded page eviction (`kswapd`, the kernel thread that frees memory by evicting pages), and TLB shootdowns, inter-processor interrupts that flush stale entries from every core's TLB when a page is unmapped.

Why do TLB shootdowns hit mmap and not a buffer pool? The virtual memory course showed the mechanism: when a mapping is removed, every core that may cache the translation must be interrupted to flush it. Under mmap, evicting a page means removing its page table entry from the process, so each eviction can interrupt every core running the database's threads; Crotty and colleagues call this a significant cost. A buffer pool keeps its frames mapped all the time. Evicting a page there means writing the frame out if it is dirty and reading another page into the same frame with `pread`: no page table entry changes, so there is nothing to shoot down.

blocks.title: Random reads: explicit I/O (fio) vs mmap, simplified

scenes.caption: From the paper's text: 100 threads doing random reads on one NVMe SSD. fio (the Flexible I/O tester, a benchmark that issues explicit reads) holds close to 900K reads per second throughout.
mmap with MADV_RANDOM tracks fio for the first 27 seconds, while the page cache still has free memory.
The page cache is full, so every new page needs an eviction. Throughput drops to nearly zero for about five seconds.
It recovers to roughly half of fio, limited by eviction overhead: shootdowns, one kswapd thread, page table contention. The 40 s end point is illustrative; phases are from the paper.

blocks.md: The paper's summary: mmap did well only on a single SSD during the initial loading phase; once eviction began, or with multiple SSDs, it was 2 to 20 times worse than fio. For sequential scans across 10 SSDs the gap was roughly 20 times. MongoDB (its original MMAPv1 engine), InfluxDB and SingleStore all moved off mmap-based file I/O after hitting these problems.

If you do use mmap, you can steer the kernel with hints ([madvise(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/madvise.2.html)):

- `MADV_SEQUENTIAL`: read ahead aggressively (fetch the next pages before they are asked for), pages may be freed soon after use. Good for scans.
- `MADV_RANDOM`: read-ahead is less useful. Good for point lookups.
- `MADV_WILLNEED`: start reading this range now.
- `MADV_DONTNEED`: done with this range; the kernel may free it, and later accesses refetch from the file (or get zeros for private anonymous memory).

`MAP_POPULATE` prefaults the whole mapping at `mmap` time instead of on first touch, `mlock` keeps a range resident so it never faults again ([mlock(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/mlock.2.html)), and `mincore` reports which pages are resident.

blocks.title: Page faults to first-touch 1 GiB of anonymous memory

scenes.caption: With 4 KiB pages, touching 1 GiB takes 262,144 first-touch faults, each a kernel entry.

Transparent huge pages map 2 MiB per fault: 512 faults, the 512x cut the kernel docs describe. The bigger lasting win is fewer TLB misses. Simplified: THP applies to anonymous memory and tmpfs/shmem (memory-backed files), not regular file mappings.

blocks.md: `MAP_FIXED` forcibly replaces whatever is already mapped at that address. In a multithreaded program another thread (or a library calling `dlopen`, which loads a shared library at run time, or `malloc`) may have just mapped something there, and you silently destroy it. mmap(2) recommends `MAP_FIXED_NOREPLACE`, which fails with `EEXIST` (already exists) instead of clobbering.

Use mmap for read-mostly data that fits in memory and benefits from sharing. When data far exceeds memory, or you need control over when writes reach disk and how I/O errors surface, explicit I/O with your own buffer pool wins.

blocks.question: You are building a key-value store for datasets 10 times larger than RAM on fast NVMe drives, with transactional writes. Which design does the CIDR 2022 evidence favor?
options: mmap the whole file with MAP_SHARED and rely on msync at commit
A user-space buffer pool with explicit reads and writes (for example pread or io_uring)
mmap with MADV_RANDOM, since it matched fio in the paper
mmap with MAP_POPULATE so all pages are resident up front
blocks.explain: MADV_RANDOM matched fio only until the page cache filled; then eviction overhead cut throughput to about half. MAP_SHARED also lets the OS write uncommitted pages at any time. MAP_POPULATE cannot make 10x RAM resident. A buffer pool controls eviction, write ordering and error handling.

blocks.question: Eight worker processes each need read-only access to the same 2 GiB lookup table on a machine with 64 GiB of RAM. Which approach uses the least memory?
options: Each worker mmaps the file with PROT_READ
Each worker reads the file into its own malloc buffer
Each worker mmaps with MAP_ANONYMOUS and copies the file in
One worker reads it and sends it to the others over a pipe
blocks.explain: Read-only file mappings in all eight workers point at the same page cache pages, so the table occupies about 2 GiB once. Reading into private buffers keeps eight copies (16 GiB) plus the page cache copy. Anonymous memory is private per process too. This read-mostly, fits-in-RAM, shared case is where mmap clearly wins.
